# Nmap

The network mapper: send crafted packets to a target and characterise it from the responses. Host
discovery, port state, service and version identification, OS fingerprinting, traceroute, and a
scripting engine (NSE) on top. It carries lab 11 of
[[cybersecurity-engineering-laboratories]] and opens lab 12.

Unlike a naive port scanner it accounts for network conditions — latency, congestion, interference —
while it runs, which is what makes its ambiguous results meaningful rather than noise.

## Six port states, and why three of them are the interesting ones

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `open` | an application is accepting connections |
| `closed` | the port is reachable, nothing is listening |
| `filtered` | a packet filter is blocking the probe |
| `unfiltered` | reachable, but open/closed cannot be determined |
| `open\|filtered` | no response — could be either |
| `closed\|filtered` | ambiguous under the scan type used |

`filtered` and the two ambiguous states are findings about **the defence**, not about the service.
They tell you a filter exists and, by comparing across scan types, roughly what it does. A tool that
only reported open/closed would discard that information.

## The scan-type family

Different TCP flag combinations elicit different responses from different stacks and filters —
connect, SYN (half-open), null, FIN, Xmas/Maimon, ACK, window, idle. Plus UDP, which is slow and
unreliable by nature because a silent port and a filtered port look identical.

**Running several is the technique.** Any one scan gives a partial picture; the *differences* between
their answers characterise the firewall. That is the general shape of
[[network-reconnaissance]]: measurements that only mean something in comparison.

Layered on top: `-sV` service and version detection, `-O` OS fingerprinting, `-T0..-T5` timing
templates, NSE scripts, and fragmentation/decoy/MTU options for firewall and IDS evasion. The MTU
option must be a multiple of eight or Nmap refuses — one of the small details the lab records.

## Speed against stealth

The lab states the trade directly: parameters exist that make a scan practically undetectable but take
weeks, and parameters that return results in seconds while generating traffic that is trivial to
notice. There is no default that is correct for both, and choosing is a decision about what you are
willing to spend.

## Version detection is the pivot to everything after

Lab 12's chain begins with a full-range `-A` scan to identify services and versions, which then feeds
CVE lookup and exploitation with [[metasploit]]. The defensive reading is the same fact from the other
side: **every banner an active scan reads is a banner an attacker can look up.**

The lab also records the scan failing to return a version for a service that was demonstrably running,
and a port not appearing where expected — honest reporting of a tool returning an incomplete answer,
which is the normal case rather than the exception. Zenmap, the GUI front end, would not install.

## Legality

The lab material states that scanning is regulated differently in different jurisdictions and that in
some, running it against infrastructure you do not own is an offence regardless of intent. All work
here was 2022 coursework against lab targets provided for the purpose.
